Sixteen-year-old Chaitanya had a history essay due and a chat assistant open on his laptop. He typed, "Explain why the salt march mattered," read the answer, closed the tab and wrote the essay in his own words. Then he opened it again to check a quote it had given. His teacher, Francis, had told the class to find every source. Chaitanya searched the library site twice and found nothing. The quote was invented. He deleted it and cited a textbook page instead.

At twenty, as an intern, Chaitanya asked the same kind of assistant to draft a summary of customer feedback. The wording was smooth, but two of the numbers looked odd against his spreadsheet, so he fixed them. He also wrote the final paragraph himself, because that was where his supervisor Usha wanted a recommendation and he wanted to practise making one.

"Did it help?" Usha asked. "It saved time," he said. "I still had to know the material to catch its mistakes."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya find when he searched for the quote the assistant had given?
qa.a: He found nothing, because the quote was invented, so he deleted it.

qa.q: How is Chaitanya's use of the assistant at sixteen similar to and different from his use at twenty?
qa.a: Both times he uses it as a tool and checks what it gives him, first a quote against sources and later numbers against a spreadsheet; at sixteen the aim is learning without outsourcing the essay, and at twenty he also protects his own judgment and skill growth by writing the recommendation himself.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel about writing the final paragraph himself at twenty?
qa.a: He felt motivated to practise making a recommendation, the part Usha wanted from him, rather than handing that skill to the assistant.

qa.q: What should Chaitanya do when an answer looks smooth but two numbers look odd?
qa.a: He should compare them with the original source, as he did with the spreadsheet, and correct them before sharing anything.

grounding: AI literacy across two ages: a teenager using an assistant for learning while verifying its claims, and a young adult using it at work while keeping his own judgment.

passage:
At fifteen, Indu felt her cheeks flame every time the teacher called on her. She was sure the whole class was staring, so she looked at the floor and mumbled. One day Tenzin, her music teacher, paused the lesson and said, "Look at the window and tell me one thing you can see." Indu breathed out slowly, looked at a crow on the ledge, and answered in a steadier voice. Nobody had turned to stare; most of them were looking at their own notebooks.

At twenty-one, on the morning of her viva, Indu's hands shook and her palms were damp. She had rehearsed her answers with her friend Baljeet the night before. Now she pressed her feet into the floor, counted five breaths and told herself, "My body is getting ready." When the first question came, she began speaking, and the shaking eased. She had decided that if it ever grew into panic that stayed, she would go to the college counsellor.

qa.q: What did Indu see when Tenzin asked her to look at the window?
qa.a: Indu saw a crow on the ledge.

qa.q: What did Indu learn about handling her body's signals between fifteen and twenty-one?
qa.a: At fifteen she used a slow breath and looked outward, discovering that few people had noticed her blush; at twenty-one she added preparation, feet on the floor and counted breaths, and read the shaking as her body getting ready.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when her cheeks flamed at fifteen?
qa.a: Indu was anxious and self-conscious, sure that everyone was staring at her.

qa.q: Why did Indu rehearse with Baljeet before the viva?
qa.a: Preparation calms nerves, and answering aloud to a friend meant she had practised her responses before the shaky, high-stakes moment.

grounding: Visible reactions with several causes: a teenager's blushing and a young adult's shaky hands, each softened with breathing, focusing outward and reframing nerves.

passage:
Age ten: Ishita and Bidisha called each other "Professor Pencil" and "Captain Crumbs" and doubled over laughing. Then a third girl joined in and joked about the way Bidisha stammered on a word. Bidisha went quiet and stared at her shoes. Ishita stopped laughing, walked over and said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"

Age fifteen: Anand's school trip was cancelled because of rain. "Great, just great," he said flatly, tapping his pen. His friend Ishita looked up from her phone and asked, "Are you joking, or actually upset?" Anand exhaled. "Upset. I'd saved up for it."

Age twenty-four: Bidisha joined a team overseas and cracked a dry joke about her own hopeless cooking. Two colleagues smiled politely; one looked puzzled. She noticed the silence, gently added, "That was meant to be funny, not a complaint," and afterwards kept to lighter, kinder jokes until she knew the group better.

qa.q: What did Ishita say to Bidisha after the third girl joked about the stammer?
qa.a: Ishita said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"

qa.q: How do the three scenes show humour being read differently as people grow up?
qa.a: At ten a joke turns hurtful when Bidisha goes quiet, at fifteen sarcasm hides real upset until Ishita asks whether Anand is joking, and at twenty-four Bidisha finds that a dry joke travels badly to a new team and watches reactions before joking again.

qa.q: What was Anand probably feeling when he said, "Great, just great"?
qa.a: Anand was disappointed and frustrated about the cancelled trip, and his flat voice covered how upset he really was.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do well when her joke met a polite silence?
qa.a: She noticed the reaction, clarified her intent gently, and switched to lighter jokes until she knew the group.

grounding: Humour that can be friendly or hurtful, sarcastic or sincere, and culturally variable, seen at three ages with check-ins on how others react.

passage:
In the college debate hall, Nandini argued that hostel curfews should be scrapped. Seema, on the opposing side, stood up and said, "Women's safety on the road at night is a real cost you haven't answered." Nandini paused, tapped her pen, and said, "You've got me there. I'd need to add better transport to my proposal." The room murmured, and Seema gave a small nod. Nandini later said the moment had made her case stronger.

At twenty-five, Nandini sat at the kitchen table with her partner Tarun, arguing about whether to rent a bigger flat. Their voices rose and the same points came round again. Tarun rubbed his forehead. "Let's step away for twenty minutes, then return to it," he said. Nandini agreed, and went to water the balcony plants while he made tea.

Twenty minutes later they sat down again with the rent sheet between them, and she began, "I think I was arguing about the fear of change, not the flat."

qa.q: What did Nandini add to her proposal after Seema's point?
qa.a: She said she would need to add better transport to her proposal.

qa.q: What do Nandini's two arguments show about handling disagreement?
qa.a: In the debate hall Nandini pauses, admits Seema has a point and adds transport to her proposal; at the kitchen table she and Tarun step away for twenty minutes, then sit down again with the rent sheet. Both times the aim is to get it right, not to win.

qa.q: What might Tarun be feeling when he rubs his forehead and suggests a break?
qa.a: Tarun is frustrated and worn out, sensing the argument is going round in circles.

qa.q: Why did the break with Tarun work for Nandini?
qa.a: They agreed on a set time, cooled down separately, and came back to the rent sheet, so the pause led to the matter being discussed instead of dropped.

grounding: Arguing productively at two stages: conceding a fair point in a debate, and a partner pair pausing heatedly and returning to the issue.

passage:
At nine, Anand tore open the report card in the school corridor, saw a 6 out of 10 in maths and felt his legs go weak. On the way home he kept saying, "I'm useless." Dinner tasted like paper, and he didn't want anyone to see the marks.

At twenty, he messaged three friends before choosing a college club. He asked whether his poster looked fine, whether his email was rude and whether his haircut was okay. When his friend Zubin said, "The poster is a bit crowded," Anand stared at the phone for an hour and skipped the meeting.

At twenty-five, his manager Kiran pointed out an error in his budget file. Anand breathed, said, "You're right, I missed that formula. I'll fix it now and check the others," and spent twenty minutes doing exactly that. He felt a small sting, but he did not feel smaller. That evening he cooked dinner and read for pleasure without replaying the meeting.

qa.q: What mark did Anand get in maths at nine?
qa.a: Anand got 6 out of 10 in maths.

qa.q: How does Anand's sense of worth change from nine to twenty to twenty-five?
qa.a: At nine Anand feels useless after a 6 out of 10; at twenty he messages friends before every choice and skips the meeting after one comment; at twenty-five he tells Kiran "You're right", fixes the error and feels a small sting without feeling smaller. Worth moves from marks and approval to steady self-respect.

qa.q: What was Anand probably feeling when he skipped the meeting after Zubin's comment?
qa.a: Anand felt hurt and inadequate, as if a mild remark showed he was not good enough.

qa.q: What could help a young adult like the twenty-year-old Anand?
qa.a: He could practise deciding first and checking with friends only afterwards, so his sense of worth comes more from himself and less from approval.

grounding: Self-esteem across three ages: worth tied to marks, worth dependent on constant approval, and steady self-respect that can take feedback.

passage:
At sixteen, Trisha sat in the school canteen when a classmate, Chaitanya, laughed and said, "People from your state are all loud and dramatic, right?" A few others chuckled. Trisha felt her chest tighten, as if she had been turned into a sticker on somebody's notebook. She put down her sandwich and said calmly, "I'm Trisha, and I'm not either of those. Ask me about myself." Chaitanya shrugged, a little embarrassed. Later her friend Pallavi caught up with her and said, "That wasn't fair to you. Come sit with us."

At twenty, in her engineering lab, someone told Trisha, "You'll top the maths paper. People from your community always do." She smiled but felt a weight settle on her shoulders. If she slipped even a little, would that prove something? After class she said to the person, "Thanks, but I still find calculus hard some days. Please don't expect me to be perfect."

qa.q: What did Trisha say when Chaitanya made the remark about her state?
qa.a: Trisha said, "I'm Trisha, and I'm not either of those. Ask me about myself."

qa.q: How are the two remarks to Trisha alike, and how do they feel different?
qa.a: Trisha is treated as a label: at sixteen, "loud and dramatic", she feels her chest tighten; at twenty, one who will always top the paper, she feels a weight settle and worries about any slip. Both times she says who she really is.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as her shoulders grew heavy in the lab?
qa.a: Trisha felt pressure and worry, as if any slip would prove something and she was not allowed to fail.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that helped Trisha?
qa.a: Pallavi caught up with Trisha, said the remark had not been fair to Trisha, and invited Trisha to sit with them.

grounding: Being reduced to a label at two ages: an unkind stereotype that makes a teenager feel unseen, and a positive stereotype that pressures a young adult, each corrected kindly.
